page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 3 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Responsible Source Adaptation

Lesson Focus

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.ADP.01 — adapt mythic, classical, or religious source material through purposeful transformation and responsible attribution.

What You Will Learn

  • Distinguish retelling, adaptation, allusion, and appropriation.
  • Identify a source’s structural DNA: conflict, roles, pattern, and consequence.
  • Transform context, viewpoint, stakes, and meaning rather than merely rename characters.
  • Research cultural or sacred context and state ethical limits.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 3 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
source textThe earlier work, tradition, or account an adaptation engages.The original folktale is the source text for the new story.
adaptationA new work that purposefully transforms recognizable elements of a source.A film adaptation changes the setting while preserving the central conflict.
retellingA new presentation that largely preserves the source’s central sequence and meaning.A retelling presents an old tale through a minor character’s viewpoint.
allusionA brief, indirect reference that depends on readers recognizing another work or tradition.The title alludes to a familiar myth without retelling it completely.
structural DNAThe source’s core pattern of roles, conflict, turning point, and consequence.The quest, trial, and return form the source story’s structural DNA.
transformationA meaningful change in context, viewpoint, stakes, genre, structure, or theme.Changing the hero into the antagonist creates a meaningful transformation.
intertextualityThe way a work gains meaning through relationships with other texts.Intertextuality occurs when the new poem answers lines and ideas from an earlier work.
attributionClear acknowledgment of the source or tradition being used.A brief note provides attribution to the traditional story that inspired the piece.
cultural contextThe histories, beliefs, practices, and power relationships shaping a source.Understanding the community’s history provides cultural context for the symbol.
sacred narrativeA story held as spiritually authoritative or significant within a living tradition.The writer treats a sacred narrative with care and consultation.
appropriationUse of cultural material in a way that removes context, exploits unequal power, or causes harm.Using a community’s story as decoration without understanding it risks appropriation.
ethical boundaryA deliberate limit established to avoid distortion, disrespect, or exploitation.The writer sets an ethical boundary by not altering a living group’s ceremonial text.

Vocabulary Application — Try It

Use each sentence’s context to place the adaptation term. Choose Check, review the result, and retry any missed item. This is ungraded practice.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 3 | Page 3 of 6

Direct Teaching: Transforming Sources Responsibly

Eight-Step Adaptation Method

  1. Identify the exact source and version.
  2. Research its cultural, historical, and—when relevant—sacred context.
  3. Map structural DNA: roles, desire, prohibition, turn, consequence.
  4. Name what your audience must recognize.
  5. Choose at least two meaningful transformations.
  6. Write a new controlling effect or thematic question.
  7. Set an ethical boundary and attribution plan.
  8. Audit the draft for transformation, respect, and independent value.

Visual Adaptation Map

SOURCE DNATRANSFORMATIONNEW EFFECTETHICAL CHECK
role, conflict, pattern, consequencecontext, viewpoint, stakes, genrenew question or insightcontext, attribution, boundary
Recognize → Transform → Reinterpret → Credit
Learning routes: color-code retained and transformed elements; explain the map aloud; or sort source elements into keep, change, research, and do-not-use.

Pause and Choose: Transform Meaning, Not Cosmetics

A source follows a gifted person who ignores warnings, crosses a boundary, and loses the gift. Which adaptation makes a meaningful transformation?

A. Rename the character, move the same events to a modern city, and preserve the original consequence.
Not the best choice. New names and scenery are cosmetic. The roles, pressure, decision, consequence, and thematic question remain essentially copied.
B. Make the character a researcher who releases a powerful model despite community warnings, shifting the consequence from personal loss to public harm.
✓ Correct—the transformation changes stakes and meaning. The recognizable warning-boundary pattern remains, but power, affected people, consequence, and the question of responsibility are newly constructed.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Transformation Test

Weak changeStrong transformation
rename characterschange who holds power and how choice works
move to modern citymake modern systems alter stakes and consequences
repeat the moralquestion or complicate the source’s meaning

Source Responsibility

  • Use a public-domain literary source or a source you have permission to adapt.
  • For living religious or cultural traditions, research community perspectives and avoid presenting sacred material as decorative fantasy.
  • Do not combine distinct cultures into a generic “mythic” setting.
  • Credit the exact version used.
  • If context cannot be researched responsibly, choose a different source.

Pause and Choose: Set a Responsible Source Boundary

A writer finds a sacred story from a living tradition but cannot access reliable community context. Which decision best follows source responsibility?

A. Keep its most striking images, remove the cultural names, and call the setting “mythic.”
Not the best choice. Removing names does not remove cultural meaning. It strips context while retaining sacred material as decoration and prevents accurate attribution.
B. Choose a documented public-domain literary source that can be researched and credited responsibly.
✓ Correct—the boundary protects both craft and context. A source with verifiable history and clear permissions lets the writer transform meaning while acknowledging the exact version and avoiding unsupported cultural claims.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Common Failures

  • Plot copying with cosmetic updates.
  • Using an allusion readers cannot recognize or understand.
  • Claiming one version is the universal original.
  • Removing cultural context while keeping exotic imagery.
  • Explaining connections instead of building them into action.

Pause and Try: Map the Source DNA

Source pattern: A gifted person ignores repeated warnings, crosses a boundary, and loses the gift.

Before opening the model, identify the conflict, turning point, and consequence. Then propose one transformation that changes the meaning—not merely the names.

Check your thinking

Conflict: desire or pride versus a protective limit. Turn: the character knowingly crosses the boundary. Consequence: the gift is lost. One strong transformation could place the pattern in a data-science lab where a researcher releases a powerful model despite community warnings; the new context changes who bears the consequence and raises a question about public responsibility.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 3 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Adaptation Decisions

Example 1 — Transforming the Midas Pattern

Public-domain pattern: A wish turns everything valuable into unusable gold.

  1. DNA: desire for value → granted power → escalating consequence → recognition.
  2. New context: a designer’s algorithm makes every online post profitable.
  3. Transformation: attention, not gold, consumes private relationships.
  4. New question: What becomes worthless when every interaction becomes content?
  5. Recognition: the causal pattern remains visible.
  6. Independent value: the new system changes stakes and choices.
  7. Attribution: note the adaptation of the Midas tradition and the version consulted.

Example 2 — Changing Viewpoint

Source pattern: A celebrated hero returns home after a long journey.

  1. New focalizer: the sibling who managed the household during the absence.
  2. Retained DNA: return, recognition, restored claim.
  3. Transformation: homecoming becomes a conflict over invisible labor.
  4. New effect: readers question who paid for the hero’s adventure.
  5. Boundary: avoid copying distinctive language or sacred elements from a specific living tradition without context.
  6. Research: identify the exact classical version being engaged.

Example 3 — Responsible Decision Not to Use

A writer finds a ceremonial story summarized on an unsourced website and wants its sacred animal figure for atmosphere.

  1. Problem: no exact source or community context.
  2. Risk: sacred meaning becomes decoration.
  3. Insufficient transformation does not solve missing authority.
  4. Responsible choice: pause, consult reliable community-authored sources, or select a documented public-domain literary source.
  5. Lesson: ethical boundaries are craft decisions because context shapes meaning.
  6. Outcome: “do not use yet” can be the strongest revision.

Model Grid

ModelTransformationEthical move
Midasvalue becomes monetized attentionexact attribution
Returnshifted viewpointversion research
Ceremonial storynone yetpause or replace source

Choose A or B: Transformation or Renaming?

Source: A ruler’s wish turns everything touched into gold, creating loss.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which adaptation transforms the source rather than merely renaming it?

A. A student gains a touch that turns objects to gold, becomes wealthy, and then loses someone important.
Weaker response. The names and setting change, but the wish, power, loss, and consequence closely repeat the source.
B. A student’s viral filter makes every image appear perfect, but it erases evidence of real people; the student must choose between popularity and restoring the damaged records.
Stronger response. This keeps the recognizable desire–power–consequence pattern while changing the medium, relationships, stakes, final choice, and thematic question.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Your turn: State the attribution and one ethical boundary this adaptation needs.

Compare with a teacher model

Attribution: “Adapted from the Midas tradition; version consulted: [identify source].” Ethical boundary: do not borrow distinctive language from a modern copyrighted retelling, and do not imply that the new work replaces the cultural history of the source.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 3 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Adaptation of Mythic, Classical, or Religious Sources

Purpose

Transform a source pattern into an original work while preserving a meaningful connection.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Your work should show deliberate choices, not just completion.

Source for Your Work

Source pattern: A gifted figure receives a warning, ignores a boundary, and faces an unexpected consequence. Adaptation setting: a student programmer creates an artificial assistant that begins making decisions on its own.

1. Plan Before You Draft

DecisionYour Plan
Character goal and obstacleWrite one clear sentence.
Key turning pointState the choice or discovery.
Meaning readers should inferName the idea without writing a moral.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach would produce stronger creative writing? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Retell the old story with new character names but keep the same setting, events, and ending.
B. Keep the warning–boundary–consequence pattern, but change the setting, motivation, conflict, and outcome to create a new meaning.

3. Apply the Lesson

Draft a 300–400 word adaptation using the source pattern above. Establish a modern setting, give the protagonist a distinct motivation, and change at least two major story elements so the work is original.

4. Revise with Purpose

Identify the inherited source element and revise one choice so it creates a new theme or perspective rather than merely copying the source.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your creative work applies the lesson skill and uses the source provided.
  • Your explanation names a specific choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Adaptation of Mythic, Classical, or Religious Sources

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: Source Pattern: The Ant and the Grasshopper

In a traditional fable, an ant works steadily to store food while a grasshopper spends the warm season singing. When winter arrives, their different choices produce different consequences. Retellings often preserve the contrast between preparation and immediate pleasure but may question what responsibility the characters owe one another.

An adaptation transforms an existing source into a new work. Structural DNA means the recognizable pattern—such as a conflict, role, sequence, or theme—that remains even when setting, character, and outcome change.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Identify two pieces of structural DNA in the source pattern. Explain why each is essential rather than decorative.
  2. How could a writer transform the ending to create a different theme while keeping the source recognizable?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which plan creates a true adaptation rather than a close copy?

A. Rename the ant and grasshopper, but copy the setting, events, and moral.
B. Move the preparation-versus-pleasure conflict to a new setting, reshape the characters’ motives, and change the consequence to develop a fresh theme.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write a 450–600 word original adaptation of the source pattern.

  1. Opening: Establish a distinctly new setting, characters, and stakes.
  2. Development: Preserve at least two pieces of structural DNA while transforming the events.
  3. Turning point: Force a choice connected to preparation, pleasure, or shared responsibility.
  4. Resolution: Create a consequence that develops your own theme.

Add a brief source note naming the pattern you adapted and a 3–4 sentence rationale explaining what you preserved, what you transformed, and why.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Revise one element that feels too close to the source. Make the transformation more original while preserving recognizable structural DNA.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
